Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters Alaska Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta says Small skiff ran out of fuel off Alaska and was helped by cruise ship even though Meta CEO’s vessel was closer Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Guardian staff and agency Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.42 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The crew of a yacht owned by Mark Zuckerberg did not hear a radio call for a maritime assist from a small skiff that ran out of fuel off the coast of Alaska, and by the time it did, another nearby ship had already rendered assistance, a spokesperson for the Meta CEO said. The Alaska Beacon news outlet reported that the skiff had issued a call for assistance through the US Coast Guard last week and a nearby small cruise ship, the Wilderness Legacy, towed it into nearby Farragut Bay in south-east Alaska and refueled it. Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Read more Although it was closer, Zuckerberg’s yacht, called Launchpad, had not responded to the call. The Alaska Beacon further reported that the spokesperson told them via email on Sunday that the yacht Launchpad did not initially hear the call for assistance. “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe,” the email to said. A passenger on the cruise ship had previously described on social media how the vessel he was on went to the skiff’s assistance, while claiming that the authorities had radioed Zuckerberg’s yacht and they “repeatedly refused to respond”. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA Youth unemployment UK retailers aim to create 100,000 jobs for young people out of work In partnership with DWP, firms such as John Lewis and M&S plan to offer 18- to 24-year-olds placements of two to four weeks Phillip Inman Tue 8 Sep 2026 09.21 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google UK retailers aim to create up to 100,000 jobs for young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years by giving them a first step on the ladder into work. In partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), more than 40 retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Pets at Home , Asda and the John Lewis Partnership, will offer Neets aged 18-24 placements of two to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”. The move comes after the former health secretary Alan Milburn warned in a recent report that the 1 million Neets in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervened. Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, welcomed the retailers’ initiative, saying too many young people were stuck in a vicious cycle of “no experience, no job”, leaving them shut out of employment opportunities. He said: “Six in 10 young people who are Neet have never had a job. Unless we can increase work opportunities, Britain’s Neet crisis will get worse not better.” Other employers signed up to the scheme include Tesco, New Look , Wickes, Currys and Greggs. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Opportunities like these can make all the difference, helping young people gain the confidence, skills and connections they need to get started in work.” The scheme, known as Opening Shift, follows the appointment earlier this year of the former M&S chief executive, Marc Bolland, to head a taskforce to tackle the growing youth unemployment crisis. Bolland, who led the retail chain from 2010 to 2016, has secured the support of retailers for the work placement scheme amid warnings that the country risks a “lost generation” without urgent intervention. Participants will continue to receive universal credit throughout their placement, mainly because of the logistical barriers claimants face when accepting short-term jobs that mean quitting and then rejoining the welfare programme. The programme was developed with retailers through the British Retail Consortium and the DWP and has 11,305 placements already pledged. Bolland, who is also a senior non-executive director at the DWP, is understood to have been chosen for the role thanks to his involvement with the charity Movement to Work, which had already helped more than 200,000 unemployed young people find jobs. He said: “My work as founder and chairman of Movement to Work showed me first-hand what’s possible when business and government work together to open doors for young people. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “Today’s announcement takes that further, creating thousands more opportunities for young people to build a future in one of Britain’s biggest industries and I’d encourage every retailer to look at what more they can offer.” Each participant will be guaranteed an interview at the end of their placement, which will vary from 16 to 35 hours each week. Retailers will offer each recruit a “buddy” to help them navigate the new role, with the aim of moving as many recruits as possible into a job should one be available, Bolland added. The DWP said it would use jobcentres to allow Neets to access the scheme. Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the Neets crisis, given the industry’s scale and reach touching every corner of the country. “Work experience is a first step, and with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the Neet crisis.” Explore more on these topics Youth unemployment Retail industry Marks & Spencer Pets at Home Asda John Lewis Tesco news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff Price rises gather pace in UK shops amid higher energy costs UK pay growth slows as job vacancies hit five-year low Unemployed young people to join AI boot camps to get job-ready Retail sales in Great Britain fall despite heatwave increasing food and drink demand Specsavers pays £12m dividend to parent company after jump in earnings Primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemployment What can Dublin teach us? In a 4-1 vote, Auburn councilors rejected a proposed ban on automatic license plate recognition systems, which sends the citizens initiative to a special election. The City Council heard warnings that the ordinance was too broad, restricting Auburn police from using ALPR-generated information from outside agencies and affecting ordinary digital photography and parking enforcement. The ordinance will go before voters in a special election within four to six months. AUBURN — Residents will vote in a special election early next year on an ordinance banning automatic license plate reader technology as Flock cameras remain up, but nonoperational. Republican state Reps. Laurel Libby and Quentin Chapman of Auburn and Rep. David Boyer of Poland initiated a petition drive for an ordinance banning ALPR technology on Auburn’s streets earlier this year after residents became aware city police had installed Flock cameras last summer without a council vote or public input. In the meantime, the use of Flock and similar cameras became so unpopular that councilors opted not to fund them in this year’s budget, though the units remain in place with hopes on part of the police department to use them in the future. The petition — handed in to the city July 30, verified by the city clerk and approved for a council decision Monday — was rejected in a 4-1 vote, with Ward 1 Councilor Rachel Randall the lone supporter. The citizens’ initiative will appear on a ballot before voters in a special election in the next four to six months. Related Local legislators submit petition to ban Flock cameras in Auburn City Attorney Dan Stockford listed concerns with the proposed ordinance, including its breadth of restrictions, its potential impact on parking enforcement and the scope of technology falling under the ordinance. Advertisement “The ordinance as drafted doesn’t apply to the city’s operation of automatic license plate recognition systems,” Stockford said, “(It) would prevent the city and Auburn Police Department in particular from accessing any external information generated through the use of ALPRs anywhere in the country or, potentially, the world.” Stockford said police may not be able to identify what information contained in outside databases was acquired through ALPRs. He said there is also potential for parking surveillance to be implicated and for regular police photography to fall under prohibited material should the ordinance pass. As suggested by one councilor, the police could hypothetically be required to revert back to film cameras. “I don’t think that it’s good practice for the City Council to adopt ordinance language that’s not well thought out and not well written,” Mayor Jeff Harmon said, “and I would urge the council to reject this and let it go to the voters.” While councilors generally agreed that concerns were warranted, Randall said it does not mean adopting an ordinance is ill-advised. “I still believe that having an ordinance in place that we can work on rather than having no ordinance in place is the best way to go.” While Councilor Belinda Gerry said she understands the concerns and voted down the immediate adoption of the ordinance, her decision at the ballot box will be different. “Given that I support our residents’ right to petition, to bring forth a question for us to either pass or send out to the voters when the vote is taken, I’m going to vote to support the citizens initiative,” Gerry said. Advertisement State representative Libby said in an email Tuesday following the vote that the council should have passed the ordinance outright and that a special election is not needed to do the right thing: “protecting Mainers from government surveillance without a warrant.” “That said, this special election is now the opportunity for Mainers to make their voices heard directly,” Libby said. “Mainers care about their privacy. They understand the difference between reasonable law enforcement and mass surveillance. When given the chance to weigh in, they will.” Boyer said Tuesday that attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union, an organization that regularly offers consultation on matters like ALPRs, drafted the ordinance language. Boyer said the council’s decision “lacked political courage.” A Flock Safety camera mounted is mounted on a light pole on the Auburn side of the Longley Bridge in February. (Russ Dillingham/Staff Photographer) Purchase this image “Towns across the state and country are removing these (cameras) and this (ordinance adoption) would’ve been the next logical step,” Boyer said. “Now we’re going to spend tens of thousands (of dollars) for an election for cameras that are already off and not being renewed. What are we doing here? And why do they have courage down in York where they’re bagging their cameras and we can’t?” York residents are set to vote on an ALPR ban in November. Auburn’s residents will undoubtedly vote the ordinance through, said Chapman following the vote. He lamented the extra cost to the city that a special election will incur. He also said the suggestion that the ordinance was poorly written was interesting considering an attorney from the ACLU drafted the language. Related Auburn council leaves Flock camera funding out of proposed budget “Flock cameras will save the day in parking garages?” Chapman asked. “Issue a parking pass. It blew my mind, too, talking about going back to 35mm cameras. … I feel like the attorney was grasping at straws, finding the most outlandish situations in which … banning ALPRs would prevent good police work.” Stockford said Tuesday his comments to the council on Monday were not intended as criticism of petition sponsors or the attorneys who assisted with the ordinance. He said his capacity as city attorney requires him to identify legal consequences of a proposed law. “The ordinance would specifically prohibit the city’s access to information generated by external ALPR systems, and that provision has potentially significant consequences for law enforcement,” he said. “If adopted, it would limit the Police Department’s ability to use information lawfully generated by other agencies when investigating crimes, locating missing or endangered persons, identifying fleeing suspects, or recovering stolen vehicles.” Joe Charpentier Staff Writer Joe Charpentier joined the Sun Journal in 2022 and covers the communities of Auburn, Lewiston and Poland.
